subject: Career
title: The Stakeholder Map
description: A 60-second lesson on The Stakeholder Map.

hook.text: You want to launch a new initiative. There are 15 stakeholders. Who matters most? A map tells you.

buildup.text: A stakeholder map plots people by two axes: their power (high/low) and their interest (high/low).

discovery.text: High power + high interest = manage closely. High power + low interest = keep satisfied. Low power = keep informed.

twist.text: The people you spend the most time on aren't always the most important. The map reveals misallocated effort.

climax.text: Draw the map before every major initiative. Update it as dynamics shift.

punchline.text: Know who matters most. Invest your energy there.

quiz.question: What does a stakeholder map plot?
options: People by their power and interest in your initiative

details.summary: A stakeholder map visually plots the people who influence or are affected by your work based on their power level and their support or opposition. It transforms abstract political awareness into a concrete engagement strategy.
details.whyItMatters: Without a stakeholder map, you waste energy on people who neither help nor hinder your goals while neglecting high-power individuals whose support is critical.
takeaways: Plot stakeholders on a two-by-two grid of power and support
High-power supporters need to be kept engaged and informed
High-power opponents require careful relationship management

faq.question: How often should you update your stakeholder map?
faq.answer: Review it quarterly or whenever a significant organizational change occurs, such as a reorganization, new leadership, or a strategic shift. Stakeholder positions are dynamic. Someone who was neutral can become an opponent or supporter based on changing circumstances.

faq.question: What should you do with stakeholders who are high-power but neutral?
faq.answer: These are your highest-priority conversion targets. Invest in understanding their interests and frame your initiative in terms that align with their goals. Converting a high-power neutral to a supporter often provides more impact than reinforcing an existing ally.
